Daniel’s framing usefully forces readers to ask what they mean by “humans staying human,” but it rests on a strong (and mostly unargued) teleological assumption: that humans have a *purpose* in the first place, and that this purpose is “survival.” In evolutionary terms, selection doesn’t optimize for a species-level goal; it favors traits that, in given environments, tend to propagate genes (often via reproduction, cooperation, and niche-building, not mere individual survival). Treating “survival” as a stable, singular purpose risks importing the language of engineering into biology—precisely the move that [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin) tried to displace with an account of adaptation without foresight or intention.

The sharper issue is that Daniel’s conflict may be a false dichotomy. Traits and “purpose” can co-evolve rather than trade off cleanly: humans already preserve survival *by changing the environment* (medicine, agriculture, law), which often stabilizes certain traits rather than dissolving them. Conversely, if “human traits” include things like vulnerability, dependence, and embodied limits, then modern survival strategies are already reshaping them—yet not always by changing purpose, but by changing constraints. That’s why debates around enhancement and “posthuman” futures tend to focus less on purpose-vs-traits and more on *which constraints we choose to keep* (a theme that runs from [Hannah Arendt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Human_Condition) to contemporary bioethics).

Finally, the post would gain traction by naming what counts as a “trait” worth preserving: cognition, empathy, mortality, moral agency, sociality, or something else. Without that specificity, “wanting humans to always be humans” becomes an empty slogan, and the claimed core conflict is hard to test against real cases (e.g., contraception, vaccines, AI decision systems), where survival, flourishing, and identity pull in multiple directions rather than two.
